extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Aristotelian ethics / philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting Aristotle's normative criteria for what counts as Friendship (Book VIII, Chapters III–XII): the species, requirements, causes, permanence conditions, and social/political analogies he uses to define and evaluate friendships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-matter of Friendship (good/pleasure/useful)
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship's proper object-matter is not everything indiscriminately but that which is good, pleasurable, or useful; friendship is directed to the good and the pleasurable (either absolutely or as good/pleasurable to the individual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes between the real good and what appears good to the individual, noting each person feels friendship toward what conveys the impression of being good to him; this distinction does not change the essential object since the truly good will convey that impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three motives / three species of Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three species of Friendship corresponding to the three objects: friendship for utility, for pleasure, and for the good (virtue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The species are equal in number to the objects and each admits 'mutual affection mutually known.' These three causes underlie the types and determine their character and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutuality and mutual knowledge as requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For full Friendship it is requisite that kindly feelings be mutual and that these kindly feelings be mutually known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being kindly disposed toward someone unknown (e.g., a conceived amiable stranger) does not complete Friendship; mutual awareness of reciprocal goodwill is part of the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship based on utility (instrumental friendship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship for utility consists in loving another for the advantage he furnishes; the friend is loved insofar as he is useful, not as he is in himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such friendships are result-oriented, liable to dissolution when utility ceases, common among older people or those pursuing profit, often lacking intimacy; hospitality is grouped with this kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship based on pleasure (hedonistic friendship)
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship for pleasure is grounded in enjoyment derived from the friend (or shared pleasurable objects) rather than the friend's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical of the young, formed and dissolved rapidly as pleasures change; these friends seek intimate intercourse and company to attain present pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect (virtuous) Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect Friendship is between good people who wish one another's good for the other's sake; they love each other insofar as they are good, not merely for utility or pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This friendship is most intense and excellent, permanent so long as the parties remain good, yields mutual pleasure and usefulness, and requires time and intimacy to establish (the proverb about eating salt together).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence depends on motive and reciprocity of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships grounded in virtue are permanent because goodness is stable; friendships grounded in pleasure or utility are transient and dissolve when pleasure or advantage changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendships are most permanent when the same result accrues to both from the same source (e.g., two pleasant people enjoying the same pleasures); divergence in motives weakens permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and intimate acquaintance required for true Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: True Friendship requires time and intimacy to prove each party a fit object of Friendship; desire for Friendship may arise quickly but Friendship itself cannot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes familiarity and the testing of character ('till they have eaten the requisite quantity of salt together') as prerequisites for perfect Friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship as state (moral choice) vs mere feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertaining a sentiment is like a feeling, but Friendship itself is a state involving moral choice and action; requital of Friendship attends moral choices rather than mere feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friendship as a state implies active agency (wishing and doing good for the friend); mere kindly feeling without action or requital is incomplete as Friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Living together / reciprocal acts strengthen Friendship; absence weakens it
rubrics_metrics.description: Living together and performing friendly acts characterize true Friendship; long absence prevents acting out friendship and may cause forgetfulness of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance does not in itself destroy Friendship but prevents its expression; protracted absence often leads to erosion of the bond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability by age and temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: Age and temperament affect fitness for certain kinds of Friendship: the young are disposed to pleasurable friendships and intimacy; the old and morose are less apt for Friendship due to lack of pleasurableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young people form and dissolve friendships rapidly, seek intimate intercourse, and are prone to love; the elderly or morose may have kindly feelings but lack the enjoyment required for close Friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality and similarity as ties of Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity (especially of goodness) and a degree of equality are ties to Friendship; equality produces reciprocity and balance between friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good men are similar and stable, neither asking nor rendering degrading services; equality is required in a certain sense, and extreme disparities of goodness or prosperity undermine Friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality in superior–inferior relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendships between superior and inferior (father–son, ruler–ruled, husband–wife) differ in kind and should have the feeling in due proportion—often the superior is the object of stronger feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different roles produce different expectations and results; equality in the strict sense of Justice differs from the sense relevant to Friendship (proportion matters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on number and exclusivity of perfect Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect Friendship is intensive and naturally tends to have one principal object; it is difficult for a person to be a perfect friend to many at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While one can please many on account of advantage or pleasure, disinterested, virtuous Friendship is rare and exclusive due to the time, intimacy, and stability required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship co-extensive with Communion and related to Justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship and Justice have the same object-matter in communal relations; friendship corresponds to degrees of Communion and the principles of Justice involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: goods of friends are said to be common; the intensity of wrongs (e.g., robbing a companion) increases with closeness; different grades of Communion (brothers, comrades, fellow-citizens) entail different friendships and justice-principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political-constitutional analogies for Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Different political constitutions exemplify different forms and extents of Friendship (Kingship, Aristocracy, Timocracy and their corruptions map onto family/political relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle maps father–sons to Kingship, husband–wife to Aristocracy, brothers to Timocracy, etc., and notes that corrupt forms (despotism, oligarchy, democracy's deflection) change the extent and quality of Friendship (despotism has little Friendship, democracy more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinship-based Friendship (parental and fraternal ties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship of kindred derives from parental relations and common origin; parents love offspring as part of themselves and siblings love each other from being sprung from the same stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These friendships are reinforced by early intimacy (parents love from birth; children later when they attain intelligence), nearness of age, upbringing together, and strength varies with genealogical distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friends wish for friend's good within the friend's nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A friend wishes the greatest good for a friend insofar as that good is appropriate to the friend's nature (i.e., one wishes the highest goods of which the friend as a man is capable, not to make him something other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle raises the puzzle whether friends would wish goods that would change the friend's status (e.g., to be gods) and resolves that the wish is for goods compatible with the friend's identity.
